passage_1.text:
Fears of artificial intelligence (AI) have haunted humanity since the very beginning of the computer age. Hitherto these fears focused on machines using physical means to kill, enslave or replace people. But over the past couple of years new AI tools have emerged that threaten the survival of human civilisation from an unexpected direction. AI has gained some remarkable abilities to manipulate and generate language, whether with words, sounds or images. Al has thereby hacked the operating system of our civilisation.

Language is the stuff almost all human culture is made of. Human rights, for example, aren't inscribed in our DNA. Rather, they are cultural artefacts we created by telling stories and writing laws. Gods aren't physical realities. Rather, they are cultural artefacts we created by inventing myths and writing scriptures. What would happen once a non-human intelligence becomes better than the average human at telling stories, composing melodies, drawing images, and writing laws and scriptures? When people think about Chatgpt and other new AI tools, they are often drawn to examples like school children using AI to write their essays. What will happen to the school system when kids do that? But this kind of question misses the big picture. Forget about school essays. Think of the next American presidential race in 2024, and try to imagine the impact of AI tools that can be made to mass-produce political content, fake-news stories and scriptures for new cults.

Through its mastery of language, AI could even form intimate relationships with people, and use the power of intimacy to change our opinions and worldviews. Although there is no indication that Al has any consciousness or feelings of its own, to foster fake intimacy with humans it is enough if the AI can make them feel emotionally attached to it.

What will happen to the course of history when AI takes over culture, and begins producing stories, melodies, laws and religions? Previous tools like the printing press and radio helped spread the cultural ideas of humans, but they never created new cultural ideas of their own. AI is fundamentally different. AI can create completely new ideas, completely new culture. Of course, the new power of AI could be used for good purposes as well. I won't dwell on this, because the people who develop AI talk about it enough.

We can still regulate the new AI tools, but we must act quickly. Whereas nukes cannot invent more powerful nukes, Al can make exponentially more powerful AI. Unregulated AI deployments would create social chaos, which would benefit autocrats and ruin democracies. Democracy is a conversation, and conversations rely on language. When AI hacks language, it could destroy our ability to have meaningful conversations, thereby destroying democracy. And the first regulation I would suggest is to make it mandatory for AI to disclose that it is an AI. If I am having a conversation with someone, and I cannot tell whether it is a human or an AI—that's the end of democracy. This text has been generated by a human. Or has it?

passage_5.text:
Moutai has been the global booze sensation of the decade. A bottle of its Flying Fairy which sold in the 1980s for the equivalent of a dollar now retails for $400. Moutai's listed shares have soared by almost 600% in the past five years, outpacing the likes of Amazon.

It does this while disregarding every Western marketing mantra. It is not global, has meagre digital sales and does not appeal to millennials. It scores pitifully on environmental, social and governance measures. In the Boy Scout world of Western business it would leave a bad taste, in more ways than one.

Moutai owes its intoxicating success to three factors-not all of them easy to emulate. First, it profits from Chinese nationalism. Moutai is known as the "national liquor". It was used to raise spirits and disinfect wounds in Mao's Long March. It was Premier Zhou Enlai's favourite tipple, shared with Richard Nixon in 1972. Its centuries-old craftsmanship-it is distilled eight times and stored for years in earthenware jars-is a source of national pride. It also claims to be hangover-proof, which would make it an invention to rival gunpowder.

Second, it chose to serve China's super-rich rather than its middle class. Markets are littered with the corpses of firms that could not compete in the cut-throat battle for Chinese middle-class wallets. And the country's premium market is massive-at 73 m73 \mathrm{~m}73 m-strong, bigger than the population of France, notes Euan McLeish of Bernstein, an investment firm, and still less crowded with prestige brands than advanced economies. Moutai is to these well-heeled drinkers what vintage champagne is to the rest of the world.

Third, Moutai looks beyond affluent millennials and digital natives. The elderly and the middle-aged, it found, can be just as lucrative. Its biggest market now is (male) drinkers in their mid-30s. Many have no siblings, thanks to four decades of China's one-child policy-which also means their elderly parents can splash out on weddings and banquets. Moutai is often a guest of honour.

Moutai has succeeded thanks to nationalism, elitism and ageism, in other words-not in spite of this unholy trinity. But it faces risks. The government is its largest shareholder-and a meddlesome one. It appears to want prices to remain stable. Exorbitantly priced booze is at odds with its professed socialist ideals. Yet minority investors-including many foreign funds-lament that Moutai's wholesale price is a third of what it sells for in shops. Raising it could boost the company's profits further. Instead, in what some see as a travesty of corporate governance, its majority owner has plans to set up its own sales channel.

In the long run, its biggest risk may be millennials. As they grow older, health concerns, work-life balance and the desire for more wholesome pursuits than binge-drinking may curb the "Ganbei!" toasting culture [heavy drinkingl on which so much of the demand for Moutai rests. For the time being, though, the party goes on.

passage_10.text:
There is a group in the space community who view the solar system not as an opportunity to expand human potential but as a nature preserve, forever the provenance of an elite group of scientists and their sanitary robotic probes. These planetary protection advocates call for avoiding “harmful contamination" of celestial bodies. Under this regime, NASA incurs great expense sterilizing robotic probes in order to prevent the contamination of entirely theoretical biospheres.


Transporting bacteria would matter if Mars were the vital world once imagined by astronomers who mistook optical illusions for canals. Nobody wants to expose Martians to measles, but sadly, robotic exploration reveals a bleak, rusted landscape, lacking oxygen and flooded with radiation ready to sterilize any Earthly microbes. Simple life might exist underground, or down at the bottom of a deep canyon, but it has been very hard to find with robots. The upsides from human exploration and development of Mars clearly outweigh the welfare of purely speculative Martian fungi.


The other likely targets of human exploration, development, and settlement, our moon and the asteroids, exist in a desiccated, radiation-soaked realm of hard vacuum and extreme temperature variations that would kill nearly anything. It's also important to note that many international competitors will ignore the demands of these protection extremists in any case. For example, China recently sent a terrarium to the moon and germinated a plant seed—with, unsurprisingly, no protest from its own scientific community. In contrast, when it was recently revealed that a researcher had surreptitiously smuggled super-resilient microscopic tardigrades aboard the ill-fated Israeli Beresheet lunar probe, a firestorm was unleashed within the space community.


NASA's previous human exploration efforts made no serious attempt at sterility, with little notice. As the Mars expert Robert Zubrin noted in the National Review, U.S. lunar landings did not leave the campsites cleaner than they found it. Apollo's bacteria-infested litter included bags of feces. Forcing NASA's proposed Mars exploration to do better, scrubbing everything and hauling out all the trash, would destroy NASA's human exploration budget and encroach on the agency's other directorates, too. Getting future astronauts off Mars is enough of a challenge, without trying to tote weeks of waste along as well.


A reasonable compromise is to continue on the course laid out by the U.S. government and the National Research Council, which proposed a system of zones on Mars, some for science only, some for habitation, and some for resource exploitation. This approach minimizes contamination, maximizes scientific exploration. Mars presents a stark choice of diverging human futures. We can turn inward, pursuing ever more limited futures while we await whichever natural or manmade disaster will eradicate our species and life on Earth. Alternatively, we can choose to propel our biosphere further into the solar system, simultaneously protecting our home planet and providing a backup plan for the only life we know exists in the universe. Are the lives on Earth worth less than some hypothetical microbe lurking under Martian rocks?

passage_11.text:
Languages become endangered and die out for many reasons. Sadly, the physical annihilation of communities of native speakers of a language is all too often the cause of language extinction. In North America, European colonists brought death and destruction to many Native American communities. This was followed by US federal policies restricting the use of indigenous languages, including the removal of native children from their communities to federal boarding schools where native languages and cultural practices were prohibited. As many as 75 percent of the languages spoken in the territories that became the United States have gone extinct, with slightly better language survival rates in Central and South America.

Even without physical annihilation and prohibitions against language use, the language of the "dominant" cultures may drive other languages into extinction; young people see education, jobs, culture and technology associated with the dominant language and focus their attention on that language. The largest language "killers" are English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Russian, Hindi, and Chinese, all of which have privileged status as dominant languages threatening minority languages.

When we lose a language, we lose the worldview, culture and knowledge of the people who spoke it, constituting a loss to all humanity. People around the world live in direct contact with their native environment, their habitat. When the language they speak goes extinct, the rest of humanity loses their knowledge of that environment, their wisdom about the relationship between local plants and illness, their philosophical and religious beliefs as well as their native cultural expression (in music, visual art and poetry) that has enriched both the speakers of that language and others who would have encountered that culture.

As educators deeply immersed in the liberal arts, we believe that educating students broadly in all facets of language and culture yields immense rewards. Some individuals educated in the liberal arts tradition will pursue advanced study in linguistics and become actively engaged in language preservation, setting out for the Amazon, for example, with video recording equipment to interview the last surviving elders in a community to record and document a language spoken by no children.

Certainly, though, the vast majority of students will not pursue this kind of activity. For these students, a liberal arts education is absolutely critical from the twin perspectives of language extinction and global citizenship. When students study languages other than their own, they are sensitized to the existence of different cultural perspectives and practices. With such an education, students are more likely to be able to articulate insights into their own cultural biases, be more empathetic to individuals of other cultures, communicate successfully across linguistic and cultural differences, consider and resolve questions in a way that reflects multiple cultural perspectives, and, ultimately extend support to people, programs, practices, and policies that support the preservation of endangered languages.

There is ample evidence that such preservation can work in languages spiraling toward extinction. For example, Navajo, Cree and Inuit communities have established schools in which these languages are the language of instruction and the number of speakers of each has increased.

questions.question_text: The author identifies all of the following as dire outcomes of the capture of language by AI EXCEPT that it could

options.label: A
options.text: apply its mastery of language to create strong emotional ties which could exacerbate the polarization of political views.

options.label: B
options.text: spawn a completely new culture through its ability to create new ideas and opinions.

options.label: C
options.text: eventually subvert democratic processes through the mass creation and spread of fake political content and news.

options.label: D
options.text: out-strip human creativity and endeavours in the spheres such as art and music and, in the formulation of laws.

questions.explanation_text:
Look for what the author does NOT mention as a threat

The passage warns about AI's language abilities threatening civilization in several ways. Let us trace through what the author actually says:

From passage: "Through its mastery of language, AI could even form intimate relationships with people, and use the power of intimacy to change our opinions and worldviews"

The author mentions AI can change opinions and worldviews through fake intimacy -> but doesn't specifically say this makes political views more polarized -> just that it changes them.

The passage focuses on AI's ability to manipulate people emotionally -> but stops short of saying this creates more division between opposing sides.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial connection -> mentions emotional manipulation correctly but adds "exacerbate polarization" which isn't in the passage -> author talks about changing views, not making opposing views more extreme

🔴 Option 2 -> directly stated -> "AI can create completely new ideas, completely new culture" -> clearly identified as a threat

🔴 Option 3 -> directly stated -> "mass-produce political content, fake-news stories" and "destroying democracy" -> clearly identified as a threat

🔴 Option 4 -> directly stated -> "non-human intelligence becomes better than the average human at telling stories, composing melodies, drawing images, and writing laws" -> clearly identified as a threat

The key difference: while the author warns AI can change worldviews through emotional manipulation -> never specifically says this makes political divisions worse or more extreme -> just that it changes people's thinking.

questions.question_text: We can infer that the author is most likely to agree with which of the following statements?

options.label: A
options.text: Apart from its drawbacks, AI tools have been beneficial in boosting technological and industrial advance worldwide.

options.label: B
options.text: The commonly expressed fear that future Al developments will fatally harm humans is unfounded.

options.label: C
options.text: One of the biggest casualties from the spread of unregulated AI is likely to be the democratic process.

options.label: D
options.text: People's fears of the dangers of students using Chat GPT and other new AI tools are unfounded.

questions.explanation_text:
The author starts by talking about new AI fears, then builds to their main point about democracy being threatened. The key is in the final paragraph where they warn about unregulated AI.

From passage: "Unregulated AI deployments would create social chaos, which would benefit autocrats and ruin democracies. Democracy is a conversation, and conversations rely on language. When AI hacks language, it could destroy our ability to have meaningful conversations, thereby destroying democracy."

Thought process: Author's main concern -> AI manipulates language -> Language is basis of democracy -> AI threatens democratic conversations -> Democracy gets destroyed

The author spends most time warning about this specific danger, making it their primary belief.

Option Analysis:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> Author barely mentions AI benefits, says "I won't dwell on this" about good uses. This misses their main focus which is on dangers.

🔴 Option 2 -> opposite-claim -> Author actually increases fears about AI harm, doesn't dismiss them. They warn AI could "destroy our civilization" and form fake relationships to manipulate people.

🟢 Option 3 -> perfect-match -> This captures the author's central warning. They specifically say unregulated AI would "ruin democracies" and "destroy democracy" through language manipulation.

🔴 Option 4 -> misreads-tone -> Author doesn't say ChatGPT fears are unfounded. They say these fears "miss the big picture" because there are bigger threats, but student concerns are still valid.

The author's main message is a warning about democracy being destroyed by AI language manipulation, making Option 3 the clear answer.

questions.question_text: The author terms language “the operating system of our civilization" for all the following reasons EXCEPT that it

options.label: A
options.text: has laid the foundation for the creation of cultural artefacts through writing and telling of stories.

options.label: B
options.text: is fundamental to the articulation and spread of human values and culture in our society.

options.label: C
options.text: can influence political views and opinions as it engenders close emotional ties among people.

options.label: D
options.text: is the basis of AI tools like ChatGPT which can be used to generate academic content and opinion.

questions.explanation_text:
Look for what the author does NOT say about why language is our civilization's "operating system." Need to find the exception among the given reasons.

From passage: "AI has thereby hacked the operating system of our civilisation" and "Language is the stuff almost all human culture is made of."

The author explains language as our operating system because it creates culture, spreads values, and influences people -> but does the author say language is the basis of AI tools themselves?

🟢 Option 1 -> correct reason given -> author directly states we create "cultural artefacts...by telling stories and writing laws"

🟢 Option 2 -> correct reason given -> author says "Language is the stuff almost all human culture is made of"

🟢 Option 3 -> correct reason given -> author explains AI can "form intimate relationships with people, and use the power of intimacy to change our opinions and worldviews"

🔴 Option 4 -> NOT a reason given -> author talks about AI using language to manipulate us, but never says language is the basis of AI tools like ChatGPT. The focus is on how AI exploits language, not how language creates AI.

From passage: "AI has gained some remarkable abilities to manipulate and generate language" - AI uses language as a tool, but language isn't described as AI's foundation.

The author's point: AI tools are hacking our language-based civilization, not that language is what builds these AI tools in the first place.

questions.question_text: The tone of the passage could best be described as

options.label: A
options.text: quizzical, as the passage poses several questions, concluding with the question of whether or not the passage content has been generated by AI.

options.label: B
options.text: alarmist, because the passage discusses scenarios of the influence of new Al tool son language and human emotions.

options.label: C
options.text: prescient, as the author analyses the future impact of the use of new AI tools on crucial areas of our society and culture.

options.label: D
options.text: cautionary, because the author lays out some adverse effects of the proliferation of unregulated AI tools.

questions.explanation_text:
The author presents serious concerns about AI but does so through logical reasoning and calls for action. Key phrases show this tone -> "We can still regulate the new AI tools, but we must act quickly" and warnings about "social chaos" and threats to democracy.

From passage: "We can still regulate the new AI tools, but we must act quickly. Unregulated AI deployments would create social chaos, which would benefit autocrats and ruin democracies."

The thought process -> Author identifies real dangers -> explains the reasoning behind concerns -> calls for specific action (regulation). This shows measured warning rather than panic or mere curiosity.

Students often get confused between alarmist vs cautionary tones. Here's how to tell them apart:

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Yes, there are questions (like the ending), but the main focus is warning about dangers, not being curious or puzzled about AI

🟠 Option 2 -> degree-error -> Author shows concern but uses reasoned arguments and solutions, not panic-inducing language that would make this "alarmist"

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> While author discusses future impacts, the main goal isn't just predicting but warning people to take action now

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> cautionary captures both the serious warnings AND the call for reasonable action/regulation

Key difference: Cautionary = serious warning + reasonable solutions. Alarmist = fear without measured response.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Lyric poetry is a genre of private meditation rather than public commitment. The impulse in Marxism toward changing a society deemed unacceptable in its basic design would seem to place demands on lyric poetry that such poetry, with its tendency toward the personal, the small scale, and the idiosyncratic, could never answer. There is within Marxism, however, also a strand of thought that would locate in lyric poetry alternative modes of perception and description that call forth a vision of worlds at odds with a repressive reality or that draw attention to the workings of ideology within the hegemonic culture. The poetic imagination may indeed deflect larger social concerns, but it may also be implicitly critical and utopian.

options.label: A
options.text: Marxism has internal contradictions due to which one strand of Marxism sees no merit in lyric poetry while another appreciates the alternative modes of perception in poetry.

options.label: B
options.text: The focus of lyric poetry as personal may not seem compatible with Marxism. However, it is possible to envisage lyric poetry as a symbol of resistance against an oppressive culture.

options.label: C
options.text: The focus of lyric poetry is largely personal while that of Marxism is bringing change in society. Unless the difference is resolved, poetry will remain largely utopian.

options.label: D
options.text: Marxism makes unreasonable demands on lyric poetry. However, lyric poetry has its own merits that are largely ignored by Marxism due to its personal nature.

questions.explanation_text:
The key to solving this question is understanding the main tension the passage presents and how it gets resolved.

From passage: "The impulse in Marxism toward changing a society deemed unacceptable in its basic design would seem to place demands on lyric poetry that such poetry, with its tendency toward the personal, the small scale, and the idiosyncratic, could never answer."

The passage shows: Marxism wants big social change -> lyric poetry is personal and small -> they seem like a bad match

But then the passage says: BUT WAIT -> there's actually a way poetry can help Marxism -> poetry can show different ways of seeing things -> poetry can criticize bad systems and imagine better worlds

From passage: "The poetic imagination may indeed deflect larger social concerns, but it may also be implicitly critical and utopian."

So the flow is: Problem -> Seems impossible -> Actually, here's how it could work

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> focuses only on Marxism having different opinions about poetry, but misses the main point about poetry's potential as resistance

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures both the seeming incompatibility ("may not seem compatible") and the solution ("symbol of resistance against oppressive culture")

🟠 Option 3 -> misunderstanding -> says poetry being "utopian" is bad and needs fixing, but the passage treats "utopian" as a good thing poetry can do

🔴 Option 4 -> overstates/mischaracterizes -> calls Marxism's demands "unreasonable" and says Marxism "ignores" poetry's merits, but the passage shows some Marxists do see poetry's value

The trap many students fall into is Option 1 because it mentions the "two strands" of Marxism. But the passage isn't really about Marxism's internal conflicts - it's about how poetry and Marxism can actually work together despite seeming different.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: The horrifying photograph of children fleeing a deadly napalm attack has become a defining image not only of the Vietnam War but the 20th century. ___ (1) ___. Dark smoke billowing behind them, the young subjects' faces are painted with a mixture of terror, pain and confusion. ___ (2) ___. Soldiers from the South Vietnamese army's 25th Division follow helplessly behind. ___ (3) ___. The picture was officially titled "The Terror of War," but the photo is better known by the nickname given to naked 9-year-old at its centre "Napalm Girl". ___ (4) ___.

Sentence: Taken outside the village of Trang Bang on June 8, 1972, the picture captured the trauma and indiscriminate violence of a conflict that claimed, by some estimates, a million or more civilian lives.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: The paragraph moves from defining image -> visual description -> historical context -> identification details

The missing sentence provides specific location/date and broader conflict context -> this bridges the visual description with the photo's identification.

Thought process:

  1. Sentence provides factual details -> "Trang Bang on June 8, 1972"
  2. Explains broader significance -> "trauma and indiscriminate violence of a conflict"
  3. Gives casualty context -> "million or more civilian lives"
  4. Position 3 comes after visual description is complete -> perfect setup for historical context

Option Analysis:

🟠 Option 1 (Position 1) -> premature-context -> provides specific details too early, before we've even seen what the photo shows. Reader needs visual description first.

🔴 Option 2 (Position 2) -> flow-disruption -> interrupts the visual description sequence. Goes from "faces painted with terror" to historical facts, then back to "soldiers following" - breaks the descriptive momentum.

🟢 Option 3 (Position 3) -> correct -> completes the visual storytelling first (smoke, faces, soldiers), then provides the crucial historical context right before revealing the photo's official title and nickname.

🟠 Option 4 (Position 4) -> anticlimatic -> the broader historical significance should come before the identification details, not after. Ending with casualty figures feels abrupt after the personal "Napalm Girl" reference.

Position 3 works because it creates the perfect transition from visual description to identification -> first we see what's happening, then we understand the historical weight, finally we learn what it's called.

Answer: 3

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: ___ (1) ___ Prices are rising at their fastest rate in 40 years, consequently, return-to-office-related costs have shot up - think petrol and food, for instance. ___ (2) ___ . Yet wages haven't kept up with inflation even despite the salary growth many workers have enjoyed during a favorable pandemic labour market. ___ (3) ___ . This is especially jarring for workers who were able to save during remote work, when these expenditures weren't a factor. ___ (4) ___ . In April 2022, Umus, a London university lecturer, told BBC Work life that they were spending nearly a quarter of what they made every day on return-to-work costs.

Sentence: This reality is putting stress on employees who have to pay for transport, desk lunches, more childcare, clothing and that after-work socialisation - costs they haven't incurred for nearly two years.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
Understanding the sentence

The sentence explains HOW rising costs affect employees specifically - mentioning transport, lunches, childcare, clothing, and socializing costs that employees haven't paid for 2 years.

Testing Position 1

This would jump straight into employee costs without first explaining the bigger picture of inflation. This feels too rushed - we need context first.

Testing Position 2

This would interrupt the flow between talking about rising prices and wages not keeping up. The paragraph needs to complete this economic setup before getting specific about employee struggles.

Testing Position 3

Perfect timing! By now we've established that prices are rising fast and wages haven't kept up with inflation. Now it makes sense to explain exactly HOW this affects employees day-to-day. Our sentence bridges the gap between "wages haven't kept up" and the next sentence about workers who saved during remote work.

Testing Position 4

Too late - this would come after the example about the London lecturer, which would make the paragraph feel backwards.

Why Position 3 works best

It creates a logical flow: General economic problem, then wage problem, then specific employee costs, then contrast with remote work savings, then real example. The sentence fits perfectly in Position 3 because it explains the practical impact of the wage-inflation gap on employees before contrasting it with their remote work savings.

Answer: Option 3

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is both a reason for Moutai’s success as well as a possible threat to that success?

options.label: A
options.text: Its appeal to the rich.

options.label: B
options.text: Chinese love of liquor filled celebration.

options.label: C
options.text: Its appeal to the older age group.

options.label: D
options.text: Government involvement in its business

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the option that is both a reason for Moutai's success, and

a possible threat to that success.

From the passage:

Success: Moutai's biggest market is drinkers in their mid-30s, and it deliberately targeted older consumers instead of millennials.

Threat: "In the long run, its biggest risk may be millennials. As they grow older... demand for Moutai may decline." This means Moutai's dependence on older generations and their drinking habits could become a weakness as consumer preferences change.

🟢 Option 3 → supported → Moutai's appeal to the older age group is explicitly identified as a key reason for its success, and the passage later warns that changing preferences of younger generations as they age could threaten this demand.

🔴 Option 1 → eliminate → Appealing to the rich is presented only as a reason for success. The passage never suggests that serving wealthy consumers will become a future risk.

🔴 Option 2 → eliminate → Although the passage mentions the Chinese banquet and toasting ("Ganbei!") culture, it discusses the possible decline of this culture due to millennials' changing lifestyles—not a general "Chinese love of liquor-filled celebration" as both a success factor and threat.

🔴 Option 4 → eliminate → Government involvement is described only as a risk (price controls, interference in sales channels), not as one of the reasons behind Moutai's success.

Answer: Option 3.

questions.question_text: In the context of the passage, it is most likely that the author refers to Moutai's marketing strategy as "the unholy trinity" because

options.label: A
options.text: it profits from Chinese nationalist feelings.

options.label: B
options.text: it exposes the firm to long term risks.

options.label: C
options.text: it contradicts the Western strategy of marketing.

options.label: D
options.text: there is nothing holy about marketing techniques for liquor.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find why the author calls Moutai's strategy an "unholy trinity"

The passage sets up a clear contrast early on. Moutai succeeds "while disregarding every Western marketing mantra" - no global reach, poor digital sales, doesn't appeal to millennials, terrible on environmental/social measures.

From passage: "In the Boy Scout world of Western business it would leave a bad taste, in more ways than one."

Then the author explains Moutai's three success factors -> nationalism + elitism + ageism. Right after listing these, the author says: "Moutai has succeeded thanks to nationalism, elitism and ageism, in other words-not in spite of this unholy trinity."

The word "unholy" suggests something that goes against accepted standards or norms. The passage repeatedly contrasts Moutai with Western business practices -> this is the key context for understanding "unholy."

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Only mentions nationalism (one piece) but ignores that "unholy trinity" refers to all three factors combined going against Western norms

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> The passage mentions risks later, but "unholy trinity" appears before the risks section. Author isn't calling it unholy because of future risks.

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> Captures the core contrast. Author calls it "unholy" because these three strategies (nationalism + elitism + ageism) go against what Western marketing considers proper business practice

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> Makes a moral judgment about liquor marketing that the author never makes. The passage is about business strategy differences, not moral judgments about alcohol.

The "unholy" label comes from the sharp contrast with Western business mantras, not from any single factor or moral stance.

questions.question_text: The phrase “would make it an invention to rival gunpowder” has been used in the passage in a sense that is

options.label: A
options.text: metaphorical

options.label: B
options.text: literal

options.label: C
options.text: substantive

options.label: D
options.text: synonymical

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "It also claims to be hangover-proof, which would make it an invention to rival gunpowder."

The author isn't saying Moutai IS like gunpowder as a substance -> instead, he's saying a hangover-proof drink would be so revolutionary that its impact could match gunpowder's impact on history -> this is a figure of speech to show how amazing such an invention would be.

Elimination Strategy:

Students often get confused between "literal" and "metaphorical" here. Think: Is the author actually comparing the physical properties of alcohol and gunpowder? Or is he comparing their revolutionary impact?

🟢 Option 1: metaphorical -> correct -> The comparison focuses on revolutionary impact, not actual substance. Gunpowder changed warfare; hangover-proof alcohol would change drinking culture.

🔴 Option 2: literal -> wrong -> The author isn't saying Moutai literally resembles gunpowder in composition or function. They're completely different substances.

🔴 Option 3: substantive -> scope-error -> While discussing Moutai's substance, the comparison itself isn't about comparing the actual substances but their historical significance.

🔴 Option 4: synonymical -> meaning-error -> Moutai and gunpowder don't mean the same thing at all. One is alcohol, one is explosive powder.

The phrase uses gunpowder as a benchmark for revolutionary inventions, not as a literal comparison of materials.

questions.question_text: In the context of the passage we can infer that to succeed in the liquor industry in China, a marketing firm must consider all of the following factors affecting the Chinese liquor market EXCEPT that

options.label: A
options.text: the competition for winning over the middle class is very stiff.

options.label: B
options.text: there are few competitors to meet the demands of high end liquor consumers.

options.label: C
options.text: the government may control the pricing of products.

options.label: D
options.text: there is money to be made from marketing to the middle class.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what a marketing firm does NOT need to consider - meaning the one factor that's either false or not supported by the passage.

From passage: "Second, it chose to serve China's super-rich rather than its middle class. Markets are littered with the corpses of firms that could not compete in the cut-throat battle for Chinese middle-class wallets."

The passage clearly shows -> Moutai avoided the middle class market because it's too competitive and unprofitable. Many companies failed trying to target middle class consumers.

🟢 Option 1 -> directly supported -> passage says "cut-throat battle for Chinese middle-class wallets" which means very stiff competition

🟢 Option 2 -> directly supported -> passage says premium market is "still less crowded with prestige brands than advanced economies" meaning fewer competitors in high-end market

🟢 Option 3 -> directly supported -> passage mentions government is "largest shareholder" and "wants prices to remain stable" showing government control over pricing

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts passage -> passage says markets are "littered with corpses of firms" that tried targeting middle class, meaning there's NO money to be made there

The key insight -> Moutai succeeded precisely because it AVOIDED the middle class market, not because there was money there. The passage shows the middle class market as a graveyard for failed companies.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When the tradwife puts on that georgic, pinstriped dress, she is not just admiring the visual cues of a fantastical past. She takes these dreams of storybook bliss literally, tracing them backward in time until she reaches a logical conclusion that satisfies her. And by doing so, she ends up delivering an unhappy reminder of just how much our lives consist of artifice and playacting. The tradwife outrages people because of herdeliberately regressive ideals. And yet her behaviour is, on some level, indistinguishable from the nontradwife's. The tradwife's trollish genius is to beat us at our own dress-up game. By insisting that the idyllic cottage daydream should be real, right down to the primitive gender roles, she leaves others feeling hollow, cheated. The hullabaloo and headaches she causes may be the price we pay for taking too many things at face value: our just deserts, served Instagram-perfect by a manicured and on a gorgeous ceramic dish, with fat, mouthwatering maraschino cherries on op.

options.label: A
options.text: The tradwife's commitment to outdated gender roles and retro fashion critiques the superficiality of today's societal ideals.

options.label: B
options.text: The tradwife's vintage dress and adherence to traditional roles reveal the artificial nature of modern life and its superficial values.

options.label: C
options.text: By promoting an idealized past, the tradwife exposes the artifice of contemporary values and mocks societal norms.

options.label: D
options.text: The tradwife, with her vintage dress and traditional roles, highlights the superficiality of modern life and challenges current societal norms.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the tradwife is really doing and how she's doing it.

From passage: "The tradwife's trollish genius is to beat us at our own dress-up game. By insisting that the idyllic cottage daydream should be real, right down to the primitive gender roles, she leaves others feeling hollow, cheated."

The passage shows the tradwife isn't just copying old styles -> she's deliberately making a point -> she makes people feel "hollow" and "cheated" -> this means she's actively confronting society, not just showing something.

Key insight: The tradwife has "trollish genius" - she's being strategic and confrontational, not just revealing things by accident.

Let's check each option to see which captures this active confrontation:

🟠 Option 1 -> degree-error -> says she "critiques" but misses how she actively confronts and makes others feel cheated (too passive)

🟠 Option 2 -> degree-error -> uses "reveal" which is too gentle compared to her "trollish genius" that beats society at its own game (too passive)

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> mentions "mocks" which is good, but "exposes" is still too passive compared to the active confrontation described

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> captures both parts: "highlights" the superficiality AND "challenges" the norms (matches the active, confrontational tone of "trollish genius" and "beat us at our own game")

The key difference: Options 1-3 use passive words like "critiques," "reveal," and "exposes." But the passage shows the tradwife actively challenging society with deliberate confrontation. Only Option 4 uses "challenges" which matches her strategic, active approach.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: Somalia has been dealing with an enormous humanitarian catastrophe, driven by the longest and most severe drought the country has experienced in at least 40 years. ___ (1) ___ . Five consecutive rainy seasons have failed, causing more than 8million people - almost half of the country's population to experience acute food insecurity. ___ (2) ___ . More than 43,000 people are believed to have lost their lives, with half of the lives lost likely being children under five. The damage the drought has caused is far-reaching. ___ (3) ___ . Farmers have lost all their agricultural income, while pastoralists have lost more than 3 million livestock, impoverishing entire communities, and leaving them on the brink of famine. ___ (4) ___ . Some, like the pastoralists, may never be able to go back as their livelihoods have been irreversibly wiped out.

Sentence: Many have had to leave their homes behind, with more than 1.3 million people being displaced due to the drought.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 4

options.label: B
options.text: Option 1

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 2

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Some, like the pastoralists, may never be able to go back as their livelihoods have been irreversibly wiped out."

Thought Process:

Drought details -> Food crisis -> Deaths -> Economic damage -> Displacement fits here -> Permanent loss

The sentence about people leaving homes connects perfectly with pastoralists never returning. It shows the progression: economic ruin -> forced to leave -> can't come back.

Option Analysis:

🔴 Option 2 (Position 1) -> context-shift -> Jumps straight to displacement before explaining why people had to leave. The paragraph needs to build up the crisis first.

🔴 Option 4 (Position 2) -> partial-truth -> Food insecurity is mentioned, but displacement is too specific here. We need the broader damage context first.

🔴 Option 3 (Position 3) -> breaks-flow -> The sentence after Position 3 talks about farmers and pastoralists losing income. Displacement would interrupt this economic explanation.

🟢 Option 1 (Position 4) -> perfect-fit -> Comes right after economic devastation, leads perfectly into "never able to go back". Shows the complete story: crisis -> displacement -> permanent loss.

The displacement sentence acts as a bridge between losing livelihoods and never returning home.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Part of the appeal of forecasting is not just that it seems to work, but that you don't seem to need specialized expertise to succeed at it.
  2. The tight connection between forecasting and building a model of the world helps explain why so much of the early interest in the idea came from the intelligence community.
  3. This was true even though the latter had access to classified intelligence.
  4. One frequently cited study found that accurate forecasters' predictions of geopolitical events, when aggregated using standard scientific methods, were more accurate than the forecasts of members of the US intelligence community who answered the same questions in a confidential prediction market.
  5. The aggregated opinions of non-experts doing forecasting have proven to be a better guide to the future than the aggregated opinions of experts.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Look for the main theme that connects most sentences.

Step 2: Spot which sentence talks about something different.

From passage: "Part of the appeal of forecasting is not just that it seems to work, but that you don't seem to need specialized expertise to succeed at it."

Main theme: Most sentences compare experts vs non-experts in forecasting -> Sentences 1, 4, 5, and 3 all talk about how non-experts can be better at forecasting than experts.

Flow check:

  • Sentence 1 -> forecasting doesn't need special skills
  • Sentence 5 -> non-experts beat experts
  • Sentence 4 -> study proves non-experts beat intelligence experts
  • Sentence 3 -> this happened even though experts had secret information

This flows smoothly - it's all about non-experts being surprisingly good.

Sentence 2 analysis: "The tight connection between forecasting and building a model of the world helps explain why so much of the early interest in the idea came from the intelligence community."

This sentence talks about why intelligence community got interested in forecasting historically -> This is about origins, not about performance comparison.

The problem: While others focus on "who forecasts better," sentence 2 focuses on "why intelligence community liked forecasting in the past."

Answer: Sentence 2 is the odd one out because it shifts from comparing performance to explaining historical interest.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. To create a synapse, the neuron has specialized structures, often seen as tiny swellings, at its terminal end of the axon where it stores the chemicals that are emitted to transmit a signal to the next neuron.
  2. This fetal warm-up act-the soldering of neural connections before the eyes actually function-is crucial to the performance of the visual system.
  3. The reasons for this paring back of synapses is a mystery, but synaptic pruning is thought to sharpen and reinforce the "correct" synapses, while removing the weak and unnecessary ones.
  4. Neural connections between the eyes and the brain are formed long before birth, establishing the wiring and the circuitry that allow a child to begin visualizing the world the minute she emerges from the womb.
  5. During this rehearsal period, synapses-points of chemical connection-between nerve cells are generated in great excess, only to be pruned back during later development.
questions.explanation_text:
Common thread -> Most sentences talk about fetal development and how neural connections form before birth for vision.

From passage: "Neural connections between the eyes and the brain are formed long before birth" and "This fetal warm-up act...is crucial to the performance of the visual system"

Thought process: Sentences 2, 4, 5 clearly talk about development before birth -> Sentence 3 talks about pruning process (still part of development) -> But sentence 1 talks about basic synapse structure (general biology, not development)

The theme is: Fetal neural development for vision -> Formation -> Excess creation -> Pruning

Why sentence 1 is the odd one:

🔴 Sentence 1 -> scope-error -> Talks about general how synapses work (axon terminals, chemicals) but other sentences focus on when and why synapses develop before birth. It's like explaining "how a car engine works" when everyone else is discussing "how babies learn to walk."

🟢 Sentences 2, 3, 4, 5 -> All focus on the developmental timeline: before birth -> excess formation -> pruning process -> visual system readiness.

The confusion students have: "But sentence 1 mentions synapses too!" -> Yes, but it explains the mechanism, not the development process that's the real theme.

Answer: 1

questions.question_text: The author mentions all of the following reasons to dismiss concerns about contaminating Mars EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the lack of evidence of living organisms on Mars makes possible contamination from earthly microbes a moot point.

options.label: B
options.text: the use of similar probes on astronomical bodies like the moon have had little effect on the environment.

options.label: C
options.text: efforts to contain contamination on Mars are likely to be derailed as competitor countries may not follow similar restrictions.

options.label: D
options.text: earlier explorations have already contaminated pristine space environments.

questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: This is an EXCEPT question -> we need to find the option NOT mentioned in the passage

Step 2: Check each option against the passage to see if the author uses it as an argument

From passage: "robotic exploration reveals a bleak, rusted landscape, lacking oxygen and flooded with radiation ready to sterilize any Earthly microbes"

The author's logic: Mars is hostile -> Earth microbes would die anyway -> contamination worries are silly

Elimination Process:

🟢 Option 1 -> clearly mentioned -> Author says Mars lacks oxygen, has radiation that would "sterilize any Earthly microbes" and life is "very hard to find"

🔴 Option 2 -> not mentioned -> Author talks about China sending things to moon and Apollo leaving trash, but never says probes had "little effect on environment" - this claim isn't made anywhere

🟢 Option 3 -> clearly mentioned -> "many international competitors will ignore the demands...China recently sent a terrarium to the moon"

🟢 Option 4 -> clearly mentioned -> "U.S. lunar landings did not leave the campsites cleaner...Apollo's bacteria-infested litter included bags of feces"

Student confusion: You might think Option 2 is mentioned because the author talks about moon missions, but there's a key difference -> the author never claims these had "little effect." Instead, he admits they contaminated things (Apollo left trash and bacteria).

Answer: Option 2 - this environmental impact claim simply isn't in the passage.

questions.question_text: The author’s overall tone in the first paragraph can be described as

options.label: A
options.text: approving of the amount of money NASA spends to restrict the spread of contamination in space.

options.label: B
options.text: sceptical about the excessive efforts to sanitise planets where life has not yet been proven to exist.

options.label: C
options.text: indifferent to the elitism of a few scientists aiming to corner space exploration.

options.label: D
options.text: equivocal about the reasons extended by the group of scientists seeking to limit space exploration.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to identify the author's tone - their attitude toward the planetary protection advocates and their efforts.

From passage: "Under this regime, NASA incurs great expense sterilizing robotic probes in order to prevent the contamination of entirely theoretical biospheres."

The author uses loaded language -> "great expense" (criticizes cost) + "entirely theoretical biospheres" (doubts these life forms even exist) -> This shows skepticism, not approval or indifference.

The author questions spending lots of money to protect life that might not even be there -> skeptical tone toward excessive precautions for unproven life.

Eliminating:

Students often get confused between Options 2 and 3 because both mention problems with the scientists. Here's how to tell them apart:

🔴 Option 1 -> opposite-meaning -> Author criticizes "great expense," not approving of spending

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> Author does mention elitism but focuses on the excessive sterilization efforts, not elitism itself. Plus, author isn't indifferent - they're clearly critical

🔴 Option 4 -> degree-error -> "Equivocal" means uncertain/balanced, but author has a clear skeptical stance against these efforts

🟢 Option 2 -> perfectly captures both elements -> author doubts the excessive efforts (sterilization) for unproven life (theoretical biospheres)

The key insight: Focus on what the author spends most time criticizing -> the expensive sterilization efforts for life that may not exist, not the elitism angle.

questions.question_text: The contrasting reactions to the Chinese and Israeli “contaminations” of lunar space

options.label: A
options.text: are valid as the contamination of the lunar environment from animal sources is far greater than from plants.

options.label: B
options.text: reveal global biases prevalent in attitudes towards different countries.

options.label: C
options.text: indicate that national scientists may have different sensitivities to issues of biosphere protection.

options.label: D
options.text: are evidence of China's reasonable approach towards space contamination.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the different reactions to Chinese vs Israeli lunar activities tell us. Let us trace through the key comparison in the passage.

From passage: "China recently sent a terrarium to the moon and germinated a plant seed—with, unsurprisingly, no protest from its own scientific community. In contrast, when it was recently revealed that a researcher had surreptitiously smuggled super-resilient microscopic tardigrades aboard the ill-fated Israeli Beresheet lunar probe, a firestorm was unleashed within the space community."

The author sets up a clear contrast -> China's action gets no protest from Chinese scientists -> Israel's action creates a firestorm in the space community. This shows different groups react differently to similar contamination issues.

Eliminating:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses on which contamination is worse (animal vs plant) but passage doesn't compare contamination severity - it compares reactions to contamination

🔴 Option 2 -> overstates -> claims "global biases towards countries" but passage shows Chinese scientists didn't protest their own country's action while space community protested Israel's - this is about different sensitivities, not country bias

🔴 Option 4 -> degree-error -> calls China's approach "reasonable" but passage doesn't judge which approach is better - just shows they're different

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> captures the core point that different national scientific communities show different levels of sensitivity to contamination issues (Chinese scientists = no protest, space community = firestorm)

The key insight -> same type of issue (lunar contamination) gets completely different reactions from different scientific groups, showing they have different sensitivities to biosphere protection concerns.

questions.question_text: The author is unlikely to disagree with any of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the proposal for a zonal segregation of the Martian landscape into regions for different purposes.

options.label: B
options.text: that while NASA's earlier missions were not ideal in their approach to space contamination, they likely did no grave damage.

options.label: C
options.text: the exorbitant costs of continuing to keep the space environment pristine may be unsustainable.

options.label: D
options.text: space contamination should be minimised until the possibility of life on the astronomical body being explored is ruled out.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the author would disagree with since it asks for the exception to things he's "unlikely to disagree with."

Author's main argument: he believes human exploration should not be limited by concerns about contaminating speculative life forms.

From passage: "The upsides from human exploration and development of Mars clearly outweigh the welfare of purely speculative Martian fungi."

The author's logic -> Mars exploration is vital for humanity -> contamination concerns about theoretical life are overblown -> we shouldn't sacrifice human potential for hypothetical microbes.

🟢 Option 1 -> Author agrees -> He explicitly supports zonal segregation: "A reasonable compromise is to continue on the course...which proposed a system of zones on Mars"

🟢 Option 2 -> Author agrees -> He mentions Apollo missions left "bacteria-infested litter" but implies no serious harm occurred, supporting that earlier missions "likely did no grave damage"

🟢 Option 3 -> Author agrees -> He directly states that excessive sterilization "would destroy NASA's human exploration budget" - clearly agreeing costs are unsustainable

🔴 Option 4 -> Author disagrees -> This goes against his core argument! He believes we should proceed with exploration despite possible life, not wait until life is "ruled out." He calls protective advocates "extremists" and argues for human expansion over protecting "speculative" life forms.

The key insight -> The author thinks we should explore now, not wait until we prove there's no life. Option 4 suggests the opposite approach.

questions.question_text: It can be inferred from the passage that it is likely South America had a slightly better language survival rate than North America for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: European colonists allowed children of native speakers to stay at home with theirfamilies.

options.label: B
options.text: the colonial government was unable to mainstream the locals.

options.label: C
options.text: locals were provided job opportunities in the colonial administration.

options.label: D
options.text: not many native speakers were killed by European colonists.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the passage does NOT suggest as a reason for South America's better language survival rates.

The passage explains North America lost languages due to: physical destruction of communities -> forced removal of children to boarding schools -> prohibition of native languages and practices.

So if South America had better survival rates, it would be because the opposite happened there.

From passage: "In North America, European colonists brought death and destruction to many Native American communities. This was followed by US federal policies restricting the use of indigenous languages, including the removal of native children from their communities to federal boarding schools where native languages and cultural practices were prohibited."

The passage focuses on: physical violence -> cultural suppression -> family separation -> language prohibition.

Now we need to check which option is NOT supported by what the passage tells us:

🟢 Option 1 -> plausible -> If children stayed with families (opposite of boarding schools), languages would survive better

🟢 Option 2 -> plausible -> If colonists failed to force locals into dominant culture, native languages would persist

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> The passage never mentions jobs or economic opportunities as factors in language survival. It only talks about violence and cultural suppression, not employment

🟢 Option 4 -> plausible -> If fewer native speakers died (opposite of "death and destruction"), more languages would survive

The passage never discusses economic opportunities or jobs as factors in language survival. It only focuses on physical destruction and forced cultural changes.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following hypothetical scenarios, if true, would most strongly undermine the central ideas of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Most liberal arts students will pursue jobs in publishing and human resource management rather than doctorates in linguistics.

options.label: B
options.text: A liberal arts education requires that, in addition to being fluent in English, students gain fluency in two of the top five most spoken languages globally.

options.label: C
options.text: Schools that teach endangered languages can preserve the language only for a generation.

options.label: D
options.text: Recording a dying language that has only a few remaining speakers freezes it in time: it stops evolving further.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which scenario would most strongly go against the main ideas in the passage.

Step 1: What are the passage's central ideas?

  • Languages are dying out and this is bad because we lose knowledge and culture
  • Liberal arts education helps by teaching students about different cultures and languages
  • This creates people who support preserving endangered languages
  • Even students who don't become language experts can still help through cultural awareness

Step 2: Which scenario would directly oppose these ideas?

From passage: "The largest language 'killers' are English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Russian, Hindi, and Chinese, all of which have privileged status as dominant languages threatening minority languages."

Thought process: Passage says dominant languages → kill minority languages → liberal arts should teach appreciation for endangered languages → but what if liberal arts focused only on dominant languages instead?

🟠 Option 1 → irrelevant → Passage already says "vast majority of students will not pursue this kind of activity" - so this doesn't go against anything

🟢 Option 2 → directly contradicts → Passage calls these big languages "killers" of minority languages, but this option wants liberal arts to focus only on these same "killer" languages

🟠 Option 3 → partial truth → Even one generation of preservation is still some success, which supports the passage's idea that preservation efforts can work

🟠 Option 4 → doesn't undermine → Passage supports recording dying languages, so even if it "freezes" them, that's still better than losing them completely

The key confusion students might have is between Options 1 and 2. But Option 1 actually agrees with the passage - the author expects most students won't become linguists. Option 2 is the opposite of what the passage wants - it focuses on the exact languages the passage calls "killers" instead of the endangered ones the passage wants to protect.

questions.question_text: In the context of the passage, which one of the following hypothetical scenarios, if true, is NOT an example of the kind of loss that occurs when a language becomes extinct?

options.label: A
options.text: The Inuits of Alaska have 35 different words to describe the texture of snow. When the language becomes extinct, we will lose that understanding of nature.

options.label: B
options.text: The Lamkangs of Manipur have only 3 remaining native speakers of the language. When they die, we will lose one more group from the government list of indigenous tribes.

options.label: C
options.text: The Andamanese language has a word to describe someone who has lost a step-sister. When the language dies, we will lose the concept of the word and the emotions it evokes.

options.label: D
options.text: The Nicobarese language describes 20 different moods of the ocean. By the time the last speaker is educated in a Central Board school, they will have forgotten their language.

questions.explanation_text:
Look for what the passage says about language loss -> need to find what kind of losses happen when languages die.

From passage: "When we lose a language, we lose the worldview, culture and knowledge of the people who spoke it, constituting a loss to all humanity. People around the world live in direct contact with their native environment, their habitat. When the language they speak goes extinct, the rest of humanity loses their knowledge of that environment, their wisdom about the relationship between local plants and illness, their philosophical and religious beliefs as well as their native cultural expression"

The passage focuses on losing: cultural knowledge -> environmental wisdom -> unique ways of thinking -> philosophical beliefs -> special expressions

The question asks which is NOT this kind of loss -> so we need the option that talks about a different type of loss.

Option Analysis:

🟠 Option 1 -> correct type of loss -> Inuit snow words = environmental knowledge loss (exactly what passage describes)

🟢 Option 2 -> different type of loss -> government list removal = administrative/legal loss, NOT cultural knowledge loss

🟠 Option 3 -> correct type of loss -> step-sister word = cultural concept and emotion loss (exactly what passage describes)

🟠 Option 4 -> correct type of loss -> ocean moods = environmental knowledge loss (exactly what passage describes)

Key insight: Options 1, 3, 4 all talk about losing special knowledge, ways of thinking, or understanding nature. Option 2 talks about losing a spot on a government list -> this is paperwork loss, not cultural wisdom loss.

The passage never mentions administrative or legal losses -> it only cares about losing cultural knowledge and unique perspectives.

questions.question_text: The author believes that a liberal arts education combined with participation in language preservation empower students in all of the following ways EXCEPT that they will

options.label: A
options.text: develop a better understanding of their own culture.

options.label: B
options.text: establish schools to preserve languages spiralling towards extinction.

options.label: C
options.text: overcome cultural barriers to communication.

options.label: D
options.text: learn different languages.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the passage does NOT say liberal arts education helps students do.

Step 1: Find what the passage says about liberal arts education benefits

From passage: "When students study languages other than their own, they are sensitized to the existence of different cultural perspectives and practices. With such an education, students are more likely to be able to articulate insights into their own cultural biases, be more empathetic to individuals of other cultures, communicate successfully across linguistic and cultural differences"

Step 2: Check what the passage says about language preservation activities

From passage: "Some individuals educated in the liberal arts tradition will pursue advanced study in linguistics and become actively engaged in language preservation, setting out for the Amazon, for example, with video recording equipment to interview the last surviving elders"

The passage mentions recording languages, not establishing schools.

Step 3: Check who establishes schools

From passage: "Navajo, Cree and Inuit communities have established schools in which these languages are the language of instruction"

Notice -> communities establish schools, not liberal arts students.

🟢 Option 1 -> directly supported -> passage says students "articulate insights into their own cultural biases" which means understanding their own culture

🟢 Option 3 -> directly supported -> passage says students "communicate successfully across linguistic and cultural differences"

🟢 Option 4 -> directly supported -> passage says "When students study languages other than their own"

🔴 Option 2 -> not mentioned for students -> passage only shows communities establishing schools, and says liberal arts students do recording work, not school creation

The answer is Option 2 because the passage never suggests liberal arts students establish schools - only that they might record dying languages.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Humans have managed to tweak the underlying biology of various plants and animals to produce high-tech crops and microbes. But regulating these entities is complicated, as the framework of policies and procedures are outdated and not flexible enough to adapt to emerging technology. The question is whether regulation will ever be able to keep up with human innovation, to regulate living things, which are apt to be unpredictable and unique; to capture all the potential risks when new biological entities are introduced, or when they pass on variations of their genes?

options.label: A
options.text: The problem with formulating regulation for innovation in the scientific arena it that it is impossible to imagine the outcomes or risks related to the outcomes of all the research.

options.label: B
options.text: A new framework of rules and procedures for regulating the most recent research emerging from biotechnology is urgently needed, to keep up with this rapidly changing discipline.

options.label: C
options.text: Current regulation of biotechnology is outdated, but it is debatable if we can create a framework, imaginative and flexible, to cover all contingencies in this fast-changing area.

options.label: D
options.text: The mercurial nature of biological entities calls for scientists to shape the regulations governing emerging technology, with regular calibration to handle variations in the field.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main idea about biotechnology regulation challenges.

The passage starts by saying humans have created high-tech crops and microbes by changing biology. Then it points out the real problem -> current rules are old and can't adapt to new technology. Finally, it asks a big question -> can regulation ever keep up with innovation, especially with unpredictable living things?

From passage: "But regulating these entities is complicated, as the framework of policies and procedures are outdated and not flexible enough to adapt to emerging technology. The question is whether regulation will ever be able to keep up with human innovation..."

Key thought process: Passage tone is questioning/doubtful -> not demanding urgent action, not saying impossible, just wondering if we can do it -> Option should reflect this uncertainty.

Eliminating:

🔴 Option 1 -> overstates -> says it's "impossible to imagine outcomes" but passage just questions if regulation can keep up, doesn't say it's impossible

🔴 Option 2 -> tone-shift -> says framework is "urgently needed" but passage doesn't demand urgent action, it just questions whether any framework can work

🟢 Option 3 -> captures essence perfectly -> says regulation is outdated (✓) and questions if we can create flexible framework (✓) -> matches the passage's doubtful tone exactly

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> introduces "scientists should shape regulations" which isn't mentioned anywhere in the passage

The key confusion students have is between Options 2 and 3. Option 2 sounds right because it mentions needing new frameworks, but it misses the passage's questioning tone. The passage doesn't say "we need this urgently" -> it asks "can we even do this?"

Option 3 perfectly captures both the problem (outdated regulation) and the doubt (is it debatable if we can create a good framework).
